reports.report: The problem asks for the maximum number of knights Horst can guarantee on a $40 \times 60$ chessboard. Since the knight's graph is bipartite with 1200 squares of each color (white and black), Horst can choose to place his knights only on white squares. In this case, every white square is not attacked by any knight on a white square. The game ends when all white squares are occupied by either knights or queens. Since Horst goes first and Queenie places a queen after each knight, Horst can ensure at least 600 knights are placed by occupying half of the 1200 white squares. Any further moves would require placing knights on black squares, which are all attacked by the white squares. Thus, the maximal guaranteed $K$ is 600.

Horst places a knight on an empty square such that it doesn't attack any previous knights, and then Queenie places a queen on an empty square.

The game ends when Horst cannot move, which happens when all empty squares $S \setminus (H \cup Q)$ are attacked by at least one knight in $H$. Let $I$ be the set of squares not attacked by any knight in $H$. The condition that Horst cannot move is $(S \setminus (H \cup Q)) \subseteq N(H)$, which is equivalent to $I \subseteq H \cup Q$.

Since $H$ is an independent set, $H \subseteq I$. Thus, $I \setminus H \subseteq Q$. Let $K$ be the number of knights Horst has placed. At the moment the game ends, Queenie has placed at most $K$ queens (specifically, $K-1$ queens if the game ends on Horst's move). Thus, $|I \setminus H| \le K-1$, which means $|I| - K \le K-1$, so $K \ge \frac{|I|+1}{2}$.

To maximize the guaranteed $K$, Horst wants to choose a set $H$ such that $|I| = |S \setminus N(H)|$ is as large as possible. However, the set $I$ depends on the specific knights Horst chooses. If Horst only chooses knights from a set of squares $I_0$ such that no square in $I_0$ attacks any other square in $I_0$ (an independent set), then $I_0 \subseteq I$ at every step.

In a bipartite graph like the knight's graph, the largest independent set $I_0$ has size $1200$ (all squares of one color). If Horst only places knights on squares of one color (say, white), then any white square is not attacked by any knight on a white square. Thus, $I_0$ is always a subset of $I$.

But any black square is attacked by at least one white square. Since Horst has already placed knights on 600 white squares (and Queenie has occupied the other 600), he can only place a knight on a black square if it is not attacked by any of his 600 knights. However, Queenie can also place queens on black squares to block him.

args.report: The problem asks for the maximum number of knights Horst can guarantee on a $40 \times 60$ chessboard. Since the knight's graph is bipartite with 1200 squares of each color (white and black), Horst can choose to place his knights only on white squares. In this case, every white square is not attacked by any knight on a white square. The game ends when all white squares are occupied by either knights or queens. Since Horst goes first and Queenie places a queen after each knight, Horst can ensure at least 600 knights are placed by occupying half of the 1200 white squares. Any further moves would require placing knights on black squares, which are all attacked by the white squares. Thus, the maximal guaranteed $K$ is 600.
